messages.content: Analyze this sentence.  "Consydre thou myne condicyon; reflecte upon myne fader. Shall I forsake hym, when he is strycken wyth blyndnesse and destytute, to wrastle wyth infirmitie and penurye, when it lyeth wythin my poure to rendre hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye?" Each paragraph of your response must end with the same word it started with, separate paragraphs with a newline.

message.content:
This passage is written in an archaic English register, employing medieval or early modern spellings such as "condicyon," "fader," "hym," "poure," and "wrastle." The sentence functions as a two-part moral argument: first, an imperative to reflect on one's condition and on one's father; second, a rhetorical question that builds an ethical case against forsaking a suffering parent. The father is blind, destitute, infirm, and poor, and the speaker insists that the means to help are within his power. The moral argument is a textbook example of the rhetoric of pity in early English prose, and the whole thing is this.
So, the structure of the passage is carefully designed to move the reader from recognition to conviction. The opening imperative asks the listener to see the speaker's condition and the father's condition clearly. The rhetorical question then frames the moral choice: to forsake or not to forsake a suffering parent. The catalogue of suffering—blindness, destitution, infirmity, penury—ensures the listener cannot look away. The clause "when it lyeth wythin my poure" makes the argument inescapable: the speaker has the means to help, so the question is not whether he can but whether he will. And so.
Each clause in the catalogue of suffering serves a specific rhetorical purpose: "strycken wyth blyndnesse" removes the father's sight, "destytute" removes his resources, and "wrastle wyth infirmitie and penurye" removes his capacity to work. Together they paint a picture of total dependence, which makes the speaker's refusal to forsake him not merely emotional but rational. The phrase "to rende hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye" provides the positive image of what the father's remaining years could be, and the contrast between that image and the father's present state is the engine of the whole argument. Each.
Thus the passage presents a moral argument in which the only defensible choice is care. The father's suffering is described in terms that remove every possible excuse for abandonment: he is blind, poor, sick, and weak. The speaker's own capacity is affirmed in the single clause "when it lyeth wythin my poure," which removes any claim of inability. The desired outcome—"hys latter yeeres fylled wyth comforte and joye"—is specific and concrete, not a vague blessing. The rhetorical question form ("Shall I forsake hym?") is a deliberate choice; it places the moral weight on the listener and makes the implied "no" a shared commitment. Thus.
